Investigating IDWT Particle Geometry — A Readable Research Draft

Updated November 1, 2026

editorial draft

Geometry and dynamics baseline: independently reviewed research through database snapshot 2975 on 30 October 2026, with the reviewed projected-magnetic-average correction. Section 5.3 adds the independently reviewed joint mass-and-ratio comparison of 31 October 2026. The November update adds the compact-support, finite shape-basin and mechanical-clock results in sections 12.6–12.8. Each retains its own action and review status; the latest connectivity and covariant-embedding proposals remain unreviewed.

This draft explains the mathematical tools as they enter the argument. It retains the original equation numbers so that a reader can compare the calculations with the reviewed source. The technical appendices provide both reproduction instructions and a combined glossary and index. Definitions there supplement, rather than replace, the explanations in the chapters.

The argument has four stages. Sections 2–5 establish the physical setting, the count rule, the numerical scales and the depth-assignment tests. Sections 6–9 examine spin, clocks, color and relative charge using explicitly stated geometric assumptions. Sections 10–12 test how some of those labels survive spatial evolution and what separate candidate dynamics can localize. Sections 13–14 put the assumptions beside one another and identify the connections that remain to be derived.

“Geometry” throughout means structure realized in the one physical spacetime: ten ordinary spatial directions and time. An algebra used to describe field components is not another place where events happen. Likewise, the mathematical terms “state,” “norm” and “spinor” do not introduce a probability law for an electron's position.

1. A Frequency Search That Led to Geometry

The investigation began with a signal-analysis question. According to the author's account, an earlier GPT was asked to examine the Standard Model particle frequencies as though they were audio data and look for harmonics. The prompt supplied neither particle geometries nor spatial dimensionalities. The subsequent dimensional assignments emerged from investigating the frequency relationships. This is the discovery history supplied by the author; an exact reconstruction of the original model's search procedure is not required to reproduce the mathematical relationships developed afterward.

The resulting proposal has a simple numerical form: a particle's rest frequency is a common frequency unit multiplied by a whole-number count. The count is obtained from arrangements of nonnegative integers and depends on a proposed spatial depth. Section 3 derives it before considering what the counted entries might represent physically. Different particle families occupy different depth assignments in this proposal.

The later question is whether those same assignments also help explain how a pattern rotates, how it carries electric charge, how its components can interact, and whether it can remain localized. Here spin concerns the pattern's response to rotation; color names a proposed three-component transformation structure associated with quark-like branches, not a visible color; and polarization describes the directional pattern of an oscillation. Their precise mathematical definitions enter before their calculations. A shared geometric choice that constrains several properties can reduce the number of separately chosen ingredients. It need not determine every property by itself to be useful in a joint construction.

Several parts can already be checked exactly. The count formula follows from elementary combinatorics. One specified way of constructing spatial channels gives three independent channels at depths three and four. An explicit field profile transforms with the half-angle rotation law associated with spin one-half, and its integrated squared magnitude is finite at all the assigned matter depths. A separate test of whether certain real spinor components admit an invariant first-order clock selects the six maintained depths within one through ten. Another construction, using six perpendicular physical directions, gives relative charge labels zero, minus one, plus two thirds and minus one third, with two equally transforming color triplets. Each statement depends on its specified construction. The chapters below define those constructions and show the calculations rather than assuming that the numerical labels already identify particles.

Each step has its own scope. A rule for transforming field components does not automatically describe a sustained particle. A quantity preserved by an isolated field equation may cease to be preserved when interactions are added. A numerical scale recipe can reproduce masses while its origin in the field's governing dynamics remains unexplained. The chapters distinguish these claims and test which successful choices can coexist.

1.1 How Results Are Classified

An exact result follows from the stated definitions and mathematical hypotheses, with a derivation given below. A conditional physical construction supplies a field, action or interpretation and derives its consequences; its additional physical premises remain visible. An empirical calibration fixes an input using observations. A proposed interpretation connects mathematics to a physical property without yet deriving all its observed behavior. An open problem is an implication the current mathematics has not established.

These categories can occur within one calculation. For example, the three-channel counting result is exact, the decision to use that complete channel as a physical source is a premise, and reproducing the observed strong interaction from it remains open. This does not make the rank mathematical result uncertain; it specifies its contribution.

2. Physical Setting, Data and Notation

2.1 One Physical Spacetime

A field assigns component values to each physical position and time. A component is one number needed to describe that field locally; it is not an additional coordinate in which a particle moves. We write a spatial point as x=(x1,…,x10)x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{10})x=(x1​,…,x10​) and time as ttt. A formula on Rd\mathbb R^dRd below may describe a pattern's dependence on only ddd of those spatial directions. Its extension through the remaining directions must still be specified before it is a complete ten-dimensional field configuration.

For example, z=a+ibz=a+ibz=a+ib can record two real components aaa and bbb. Multiplication by iii rotates that pair to (−b,a)(-b,a)(−b,a); it does not create a complex physical dimension. Where pairs of spatial axes are grouped in the same notation, both axes remain ordinary real directions in the same space.

The physical setting is ten ordinary spatial dimensions plus time. All spatial directions are of the same physical kind. A pattern's depth d describes its dimensional involvement within that shared space. It does not introduce a second space, an internal physical dimension, a compactified direction or a separate manifold for each particle family.

Complex coordinates below encode pairs of real field components or paired ordinary spatial directions. Later algebraic constructions and finite lists of coefficients are mathematical descriptions of the field; they are not additional places in which physical events occur. Every field equation must ultimately act on the single physical field, Psi_infinity, on this spacetime.

A localized pattern is concentrated near a spatial region, possibly with tails that decay rather than end abruptly. Its internal field shape is distinct from the position of the whole pattern. For the electron, the project's existing orbit-plus-precession picture concerns literal motion around a nucleus through the surrounding physical space. The proposed trajectory uses four directions within that six-dimensional setting; it does not reduce the electron's own six-dimensional structure to four.

There are no mediator particles in the proposed physical interpretation. Interaction kernels describe responses of the same field. Electrons retain literal deterministic trajectories in their six physical spatial directions. Their internal classical field structure, their external position and time-averaged detector registration are distinct. None of the norms or integrals below postulates a probability cloud or a Born position law.

A few conventions will recur. A vector collects components; a matrix acts linearly on them. An operator is a rule acting on a field or its components. A matrix operator acts at each position, while a differential operator also differentiates the spatial dependence. The identity III leaves its input unchanged. These operations do not supply position probabilities.

An eigenvector of an operator retains its direction when the operator acts; the multiplying number is its eigenvalue. An eigenspace collects vectors with the same eigenvalue, and its dimension is the multiplicity of that value. The rank of a map counts its independent outputs, while its kernel consists of inputs mapped to zero. Two operators commute if their order does not matter: [A,B]=AB−BA=0[A,B]=AB-BA=0[A,B]=AB−BA=0. Their anticommutator is {A,B}=AB+BA\{A,B\}=AB+BA{A,B}=AB+BA. A projector PPP, satisfying P2=PP^2=PP2=P, retains a specified component subspace. Projecting a description does not by itself prove that the omitted components stay absent under evolution.

A trace adds a matrix's diagonal entries. A determinant measures the signed volume scaling of a linear map; it vanishes when the relevant columns are linearly dependent. For complex entries it also carries phase information, interpreted throughout as algebra of paired real components. An inner product, such as u†vu^\dagger vu†v, measures overlap; zero overlap means orthogonality. Tensor products, written ⊗\otimes⊗, keep two sets of component labels simultaneously. They do not add physical spatial directions. Further specialized notation is defined where it is first needed.

3. The Simplex Count and the Mass Rule

3.1 Counting the Configurations

A polynomial is a sum of terms such as 111, x1x_1x1​, x1x2x_1x_2x1​x2​ or x22x_2^2x22​. Each such term is a monomial. Its total degree is the sum of its powers: x12x2x_1^2x_2x12​x2​ has degree three. Counting all monomials up to degree kkk gives a finite set of labels without choosing their coefficients or amplitudes.

For a small example, in two coordinates and through degree two the labels correspond to 1,x1,x2,x12,x1x2,x221,x_1,x_2,x_1^2,x_1x_2,x_2^21,x1​,x2​,x12​,x1​x2​,x22​. There are six. The general calculation below counts the exponent tuples rather than writing each monomial. The notation N0\mathbb N_0N0​ includes zero, #\## means the number of elements, and (ab)=a!/[b!(a−b)!]\binom ab=a!/[b!(a-b)!](ba​)=a!/[b!(a−b)!] is a binomial coefficient.

Let P_{<=k}(R^d) be the real polynomials of total degree at most k in d ordinary spatial coordinates. Its monomial labels are

Kk,d={(a1,…,ad)∈N0d:a1+⋯+ad≤k}.(3.1) \mathcal K_{k,d}=\{(a_1,\ldots,a_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d: a_1+\cdots+a_d\le k\}. \tag{3.1} Kk,d​={(a1​,…,ad​)∈N0d​:a1​+⋯+ad​≤k}.(3.1)

To count terms of exactly degree rrr, imagine distributing rrr identical marks among ddd labeled slots. Separators distinguish the slots, including empty ones. This “stars and bars” count is the binomial coefficient in (3.2). The notation ∣a∣|a|∣a∣ here means a1+⋯+ada_1+\cdots+a_da1​+⋯+ad​, not a physical distance.

For total degree r, stars and bars gives

#{∣a∣=r}=(r+d−1d−1).(3.2) \#\{|a|=r\}=\binom{r+d-1}{d-1}. \tag{3.2} #{∣a∣=r}=(d−1r+d−1​).(3.2)

Introduce the slack integer a_0=k-|a|. The inequality becomes an equality in d+1 nonnegative integer entries. The slack label is bookkeeping; it is not another spatial direction. Therefore

C=S(n,d)=∑r=0n−1(r+d−1d−1)=(n+d−1d)=(k+dd).(3.3) \boxed{C=S(n,d)=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\binom{r+d-1}{d-1} =\binom{n+d-1}{d}=\binom{k+d}{d}.} \tag{3.3} C=S(n,d)=r=0∑n−1​(d−1r+d−1​)=(dn+d−1​)=(dk+d​).​(3.3)

Equivalently, this counts lattice points in a dilated simplex. It can also be used as an integrated density of available polynomial or oscillator labels. Those are equivalent counts, not proof that every label is an occupied physical oscillator.

A simplex generalizes a line segment, triangle and tetrahedron to higher dimensions. In this count it is the region of allowed nonnegative exponent labels whose sum is bounded. Counting lattice points in that region does not establish that the particle itself has a simplex-shaped body. An integrated density of states, or IDOS, is a cumulative count of available states through a cutoff. Availability and physical occupation are separate questions.

The next identities explain why the count is restrictive. Pascal recursion divides the same set into two smaller sets. The adjacent-level ratio says exactly how far the next allowed count lies above the present one. The final asymptotic formula describes growth at large nnn; the symbol ∼\sim∼ means that the ratio tends to one, not that the two expressions are exactly equal at finite nnn.

Pascal recursion and the adjacent-level ratios are exact:

S(n,d)=S(n,d−1)+S(n−1,d),S(n+1,d)S(n,d)=n+dn,(3.4) S(n,d)=S(n,d-1)+S(n-1,d),\qquad \frac{S(n+1,d)}{S(n,d)}=\frac{n+d}{n}, \tag{3.4} S(n,d)=S(n,d−1)+S(n−1,d),S(n,d)S(n+1,d)​=nn+d​,(3.4)

3.3 How Equal-Frequency Portions Can Produce a Count Multiplier

A portion is the proposed physical part of a pattern that performs one cycle at the common fundamental. A phase specifies where it is in that cycle. Fixed phase differences mean that portions remain synchronized in frequency, even when they reach a given stage at different times. “Equally splayed” phases are evenly spaced through one full cycle. A Fourier expansion decomposes a waveform mathematically into sinusoidal terms; it does not assert that separate objects oscillate at all those frequencies.

The current portion hypothesis uses C oscillators of the same fundamental within one particle. Fourier terms describe their combined waveform; they are not C independently resonating higher modes.

Let T_0 be the common fundamental period. If each portion contributes one registered event per cycle, additive registration gives

lim⁡T→∞Nevents(T)T=CT0,(3.7) \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{\rm events}(T)}{T}=\frac C{T_0}, \tag{3.7} T→∞lim​TNevents​(T)​=T0​C​,(3.7)

for fixed phase offsets, including uneven offsets. Counting remains valid without a perfectly uniform external repetition pattern. It presumes that the physical observable registers the events additively.

Equation (3.7) concerns an average event count. Unevenly spaced events can give the same long-time rate without forming a uniform repeating signal. The next calculation asks for the stronger property of an exact repeated waveform. The fractional part {x}=x−⌊x⌋\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor{x}=x−⌊x⌋ rises linearly from zero to one before resetting; subtracting 1/21/21/2 centers it about zero. The floor ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor⌊x⌋ is the greatest integer not exceeding xxx.

For equally splayed ideal sawtooths, a stronger waveform identity holds. Define s(x)={x}-1/2 with a consistent value at resets. Then

∑r=0C−1s(x+r/C)=s(Cx).(3.8) \boxed{\sum_{r=0}^{C-1}s(x+r/C)=s(Cx).} \tag{3.8} r=0∑C−1​s(x+r/C)=s(Cx).​(3.8)

To prove it, write the left side as Cx+(C-1)/2 minus sum floor(x+r/C) minus C/2, and use sum floor(x+r/C)=floor(Cx). This gives Cx-floor(Cx)-1/2. The sum has C resets per fundamental period. Equally splayed sinusoids instead sum to zero for C >= 2; the waveform and registration matter.

The identity and event-rate result are exact under their respective definitions. The claim that a sustained field pattern contains exactly S(n,d) such portions, and that its registered rate is its physical mass frequency, is the physical mechanism to establish. Neither the simplex count nor phase locking alone selects an occupied n. Adding one portion changes C by one; it does not prove that the new configuration is sustained.

A number near such a mean can motivate a question about dynamics, but the arithmetic alone does not identify a physical mixed state. The bottom comparison is retained with precisely that limited status.

5. How the Spectrum Restricts the Depth Assignments

5.1 Ratios and Fixed-Index Diagnostics

A common scale can move a whole family's mass ladder up or down, but cannot change the ratios of its rungs. This makes within-family ratios useful tests of the depth assignment. Two different searches must be distinguished: this subsection keeps the reported level labels fixed while changing depth; the next permits all positive integer labels while retaining the shared scale rules and complete family assignments.

Within one family the scale cancels:

mimj=S(ni,d)S(nj,d).(5.1) \frac{m_i}{m_j}=\frac{S(n_i,d)}{S(n_j,d)}. \tag{5.1} mj​mi​​=S(nj​,d)S(ni​,d)​.(5.1)

For example,

mμme=383838018564=351517.(5.2) \frac{m_\mu}{m_e}=\frac{3838380}{18564}=\frac{3515}{17}. \tag{5.2} me​mμ​​=185643838380​=173515​.(5.2)

The electron and muon are both high counts of their common fundamental; neither is that fundamental. At the muon label the next count is 17.14 percent higher and the preceding count 15 percent lower. The much smaller archived mass mismatch cannot be removed by moving one rung. Changing mu_6 instead also changes the electron.

The logarithm measures multiplicative discrepancies: being a factor above or below a value is treated symmetrically. In (5.3), rrr is the number of family entries, μ^d\widehat\mu_dμ​d​ is the best common scale for this diagnostic, and ϵd\epsilon_dϵd​ is their root-mean-square logarithmic discrepancy. Optimizing this comparison scale is a diagnostic operation; it does not replace the electron-based prescription of section 4.

A ratio diagnostic can hold the stated indices fixed and optimize a common scale for each trial depth. With benchmark masses M_i and counts C_i(d),

log⁡μ^d=1r∑ilog⁡(Mi/Ci(d)),ϵd2=1r∑i[log⁡μ^dCi(d)Mi]2.(5.3) \log\widehat\mu_d=\frac1r\sum_i\log(M_i/C_i(d)),\qquad \epsilon_d^2=\frac1r\sum_i\left[\log\frac{\widehat\mu_dC_i(d)}{M_i}\right]^2. \tag{5.3} logμ​d​=r1​i∑​log(Mi​/Ci​(d)),ϵd2​=r1​i∑​[logMi​μ​d​Ci​(d)​]2.(5.3)

Scanning integer depths 1 through 15 gives minima at 2 for W/Z/H, 3 for down/strange, 4 for up/charm/top and 6 for electron/muon. Bottom is excluded from the ordinary down/strange ratio diagnostic. The neutrino ratio at its fixed triple favors five; its neighboring-depth values are about 0.05550 at four and 0.01686 at six. The tau comparison

mτ(d)=meS(23,d)S(13,6)(5.4) m_\tau(d)=m_e\frac{S(23,d)}{S(13,6)} \tag{5.4} mτ​(d)=me​S(13,6)S(23,d)​(5.4)

favors ten only with the shared charged-lepton unit retained. A free per-depth tau scale would fit that single mass at every depth.

5.2 A Complete Assignment Theorem with Unrestricted Positive Indices

An exhaustive assignment statement needs a specified set of permitted alternatives. Here a block is a whole particle family, kept together when moved to another depth. “Bijectively” means that each block occupies one of the listed depths and each depth is used once. The proof also keeps the numerical scale recipe. It is therefore stronger than the preceding fixed-index scan, but is not a theorem about every conceivable mass formula.

The proof uses monotonicity: at fixed depth the count increases strictly with positive integer nnn. Once a target is trapped between two neighboring predictions, all other integers are excluded on that side. Fourth powers remove the radicals in the scale ratios, allowing the decisive inequalities to be checked with exact rational numbers rather than rounding-dependent comparisons.

A stronger test moves the intact blocks (WZH, dsb, uct, e-mu, tau) bijectively among {2,3,4,6,10}. It retains the scale prescription, the exact electron reference and the common electron/tau unit, and permits every particle any positive integer index. It is not an arbitrary finite scan.

Put a_d = mu_d/m_e. Their fourth powers are rational:

a24=28902,a34=7168,a44=25639375,a64=a104=1185644.(5.5) a_2^4=2890^2,\quad a_3^4=7168,\quad a_4^4=\frac{256}{39375},\quad a_6^4=a_{10}^4=\frac1{18564^4}. \tag{5.5} a24​=28902,a34​=7168,a44​=39375256​,a64​=a104​=1856441​.(5.5)

The electron equation a_d S(n,d)=1 excludes depths two and three because their first rungs exceed one. At four, one lies strictly between a_4 and 5a_4; at ten, 18564 lies strictly between S(7,10)=8008 and S(8,10)=19448. At six the unique exact solution is S(13,6)=18564. Strict monotonicity covers all other positive indices. Hence electron/muon is at six. Shared unit and distinct depths then put tau at ten.

Only depths two, three and four remain. At three the W benchmark lies between the n = 45 and 46 predictions; their fourth-power ratios are below 81/100 and above 26/25. At four it lies between n = 58 and 59, with fourth-power ratios below 4/5 and above 41/40. These bracket bounds exclude even a 0.5 percent W tolerance at either depth. Thus W/Z/H is at two. The first up-type rung at three exceeds twice the up benchmark, so even a 100 percent tolerance forces that family to four. The remaining down-type block is at three. Every certificate uses the exact archived decimal inputs as rationals, not floating-point accept/reject tests.

A bracket certificate records inequalities that locate the answer, rather than merely reporting the outcome of a search. For nearest logarithmic distance, the boundary between two positive predictions is their geometric mean. Squaring the target therefore gives the neighboring-product inequalities in (5.6). This is why the proof can cover arbitrarily large positive indices without inspecting each one.

At fixed depth, the unique nearest logarithmic rung n_star > 1 is certified by

P(n⋆−1)P(n⋆)<M2<P(n⋆)P(n⋆+1),P(n)=meadS(n,d).(5.6) P(n_\star-1)P(n_\star)<M^2<P(n_\star)P(n_\star+1),\qquad P(n)=m_e a_d S(n,d). \tag{5.6} P(n⋆​−1)P(n⋆​)<M2<P(n⋆​)P(n⋆​+1),P(n)=me​ad​S(n,d).(5.6)

Only the upper condition is needed at n_star = 1. Taking fourth powers reduces these inequalities to rational arithmetic with (5.5). They certify every maintained comparison index, including n = 17 as the unresolved ordinary bottom control. Doubling an upper index and binary-searching the bracket also finds the nearest rung without an arbitrary index cutoff.

The resulting theorem is conditional: under this scale law, intact blocks, distinct occupied depths and shared lepton reference, the maintained arrangement uniquely matches or improves every individual maintained accuracy. It does not prove uniqueness under every possible scale law, family regrouping or physical theory. It supplies a concrete joint test to combine with the separately derived property constraints.

5.3 Joint Absolute-Mass and Ratio Accuracy

The statistical comparison requires every selected mass to retain its achieved absolute accuracy and every within-family ratio to retain its achieved accuracy. Similar signed mass offsets can cancel in a ratio, so acceptable absolute errors alone do not necessarily preserve that ratio match. These requirements are imposed together on one mass list.

A joint calculation retains both, using the unchanged mass prescription P=m_e a_d C(n,d), C(n,d)=binomial(n+d−1,d), with the coefficients and reference counts given in section 4. The electron is the sole anchor. W, down and up are scored targets, as are Z, Higgs, strange, charm, top, muon and tau. No sector scale is independently fitted. Bottom remains an unresolved ordinary-rung exception; neutrino absolute masses require separate calibration and are not included in this positive-mass test.

All five blocks may move among the specified depths before the exact electron-reference and common-lepton-scale conditions are applied. As established in section 5.2, these equations leave six admissible permutations of WZH, down/strange and up/charm/top over depths two, three and four, with electron/muon at six and tau at ten. The integer search includes every allowed joint tuple, including repeated and non-nearest indices where relevant.

For each nonanchor label, let r_i=log(P_i^*/M_i) be the signed residual of its maintained prediction against the archived central mass. Freeze the actual achieved absolute and ratio bounds

δi=∣ri∣,ηij=∣rj−ri∣.(J1) \delta_i=|r_i|,\qquad \eta_{ij}=|r_j-r_i|. \tag{J1} δi​=∣ri​∣,ηij​=∣rj​−ri​∣.(J1)

A trial spectrum passes if some single admissible complete assignment and some joint index tuple satisfy

∣log⁡PiMitrial∣≤δifor every scored mass,∣log⁡Pj/PiMjtrial/Mitrial∣≤ηijfor every within-family pair.(J2) \left|\log\frac{P_i}{M_i^{\rm trial}}\right|\le\delta_i \quad\hbox{for every scored mass}, \qquad \left|\log\frac{P_j/P_i}{M_j^{\rm trial}/M_i^{\rm trial}}\right| \le\eta_{ij} \quad\hbox{for every within-family pair}. \tag{J2} ​logMitrial​Pi​​​≤δi​for every scored mass,​logMjtrial​/Mitrial​Pj​/Pi​​​≤ηij​for every within-family pair.(J2)

The electron residual is zero. Its ratios with muon and tau duplicate their absolute bounds, while tau/muon supplies a further joint constraint. All pair strips are imposed together; their probabilities are not multiplied as independent evidence.

A looser match still supplies its own constraint. Under the same reference ensemble and allowed search, adding a requirement cannot increase the accepted fraction: the joint accepted set is contained in the set obtained by dropping that requirement. Thus the looser top bound does not relax the tighter muon or boson bounds. Ratio constraints can further reduce the same accepted set; they are not independent extra probability factors.

The bounds use the central residuals themselves, without replacing them by experimental uncertainty floors. For example, the muon absolute log bound is 0.00001730021744; the Z/W ratio bound is 0.0003373485332; and the Higgs/Z ratio bound is 0.00006753194134. Full values, empirical definitions and quoted errors are supplied in the reproducibility packet. This tests achieved central numerical proximity, not a claim that every formula prediction agrees within measurement errors.

For a declared reference ensemble, fix the electron and draw the ten other log mass ratios uniformly from 0 to log R. Sort within WZH, down/strange, up/charm/top and the muon/tau pair. All ten nonanchor masses remain randomized and scored. The resulting density is 144/(log R)^10 on the ordered region. This distribution is an explicit numerical comparison, not a physical law for possible masses.

The acceptance region is too small to estimate efficiently by waiting for ordinary random spectra to pass. Instead, the calculation samples the component acceptance regions directly and corrects their sampling density. For the actual signed-residual ordering, the full set of absolute and ratio constraints is exactly a box in each family's first residual and successive residual differences. The coordinate transformation has determinant one; its common ten-variable box volume is V=1.0409457956707493×10^-29.

Let Q be the number of permitted component boxes and K(x) the number containing a sampled mass list x, counting all rung tuples and all six assignments. Uniform sampling of the equal-volume boxes gives density K/(QV). The exact union identity is therefore

p=144QV(log⁡R)10E[1ordered window(X)K(X)].(J3) p=\frac{144QV}{(\log R)^{10}} \mathbb E\left[\frac{\mathbf1_{\rm ordered\ window}(X)}{K(X)}\right]. \tag{J3} p=(logR)10144QV​E[K(X)1ordered window​(X)​].(J3)

The factor 1/K accounts for overlapping rungs and assignments, rather than approximating a union probability by an expected number of matches. Counting all joint choices is essential: actual examples pass through a non-nearest rung while every complete assignment using independently nearest rungs fails the ratio constraints.

Every positive integer rung whose acceptance band can reach the stated mass window is included. Strict increase of C shows that a label/depth rung cannot contribute after a_d C(n,d)>R exp(delta_i). Checking the last included and first excluded indices gives complete caps 194 for R=10^6 and 616 for R=10^7. These are completeness bounds for the stated windows, not a physical selection law or a search over unspecified coefficient prescriptions.

Electron-only reference window Index domain Estimated joint coverage Conservative interval
1…10^6 electron masses Every relevant rung; n≤194 suffices 2.837×10^-20 [2.673, 2.983]×10^-20
1…10^7 electron masses Every relevant rung; n≤616 suffices 7.328×10^-18 [6.709, 7.719]×10^-18

Each complete-window branch used a fixed one million importance draws. Independent Bernoulli thinning by 1/K produced 4,864 and 3,066 successes. Finite-sample Chernoff bounds, adjusted across all computed branches, supply at least 99% simultaneous sampling coverage; the displayed intervals are rounded outward and also include a separately stated conservative numerical-arithmetic guard. That guard is supported by high-precision checks and an explicit perturbation bound, not formal directed-rounding arithmetic. The arithmetic enlargement is conditional on the stated floating-error budget; the 99% guarantee concerns sampling under the fixed event, not a formally certified combined arithmetic enclosure. The sampled overlap multiplicity reaches 41 in the wider window, so omitting overlap correction would be material.

The result is retrospective conditional coverage, not a global discovery p-value. The thresholds are drawn from the observed residual vector, and the numerical prescription was developed with the masses known. This calculation does not reconstruct the historical search over coefficient laws, family choices, exclusions and formulas. It also does not supply a probability that IDWT is true. Widening the reference window admits denser high-index ladders and changes the coverage substantially, as the table shows.

What the calculation establishes is narrower: under the fixed electron-based prescription, all allowed complete assignments and relevant joint rung choices, the selected central mass matches and their ratio cancellations occupy a very small part of the stated reference distribution. This supports investigating the constrained numerical pattern together with the geometric constructions. Their shared spin, charge and depth results must not be multiplied as independent probability factors. Deriving the coefficient law, selecting and sustaining the occupied counts, resolving bottom and supplying a neutrino absolute scale remain open physical questions.

The full method and reproduction appendix supplies the exact inputs, signed-residual bounds, code, union estimator and verification scope.

6. A Spatial Field Pattern with Spin One-Half

The spin result concerns how an entire spatial pattern changes when rotated, including its dependence on position. The explicit profile below carries the half-angle law associated with spin one-half. Whether its squared magnitude integrates to a finite value also gives a useful depth comparison.

6.1 The Profile and Its Equation

A spinor is a set of field components with a specified response to spatial rotations. It differs from an ordinary vector: its rotation rule can change sign after a full 2π2\pi2π turn and return after 4π4\pi4π. That transformation rule is an assumption about the candidate field, not a probability interpretation or a claim that a tiny rigid object literally turns through twice the angle.

The group SO(d)SO(d)SO(d) consists of length- and orientation-preserving rotations of ddd real spatial directions. Its double cover, Spin(d)Spin(d)Spin(d), keeps the extra sign information required for spinors. A representation states how these transformations act on component values. Two descriptions can use different numbers of components while representing the same physical rotation group. No component count changes the number of physical directions.

A Clifford algebra is an algebra of matrices whose products encode the Euclidean inner product. Here its defining rule is γiγj+γjγi=2δijI\gamma_i\gamma_j+\gamma_j\gamma_i=2\delta_{ij}Iγi​γj​+γj​γi​=2δij​I, with δij=1\delta_{ij}=1δij​=1 for equal indices and zero otherwise. It implies that the square of the matrix γ⋅x=∑iγixi\gamma\cdot x=\sum_i\gamma_i x_iγ⋅x=∑i​γi​xi​ is r2Ir^2Ir2I. A Hermitian matrix equals its conjugate transpose. These properties make it possible to combine spatial derivatives and spinor components consistently in the Dirac operator DDD.

The proposed profile below has a radial envelope, which decreases with distance rrr, and a coordinate-dependent spinor factor. The constant unit spinor χ\chiχ is its seed: it specifies the component orientation of the pattern. The parameter aaa controls its spatial scale and AAA its magnitude. This profile is sometimes called a bubble; that term refers to the explicit localized shape, not a material boundary or an extra space.

Use Hermitian Euclidean Clifford matrices satisfying {γi,γj}=2δijI\{\gamma_i,\gamma_j\}=2\delta_{ij}I{γi​,γj​}=2δij​I, and let D=−iγi∂iD=-i\gamma_i\partial_iD=−iγi​∂i​. With r=∣x∣r=|x|r=∣x∣, a length a>0a>0a>0, a unit constant spinor χ\chiχ, and positive amplitude AAA, set

ψχ(x)=A(1+r2/a2)−d/2(I+iγ⋅x/a)χ.(6.1) \psi_\chi(x)=A(1+r^2/a^2)^{-d/2}(I+i\gamma\cdot x/a)\chi. \tag{6.1} ψχ​(x)=A(1+r2/a2)−d/2(I+iγ⋅x/a)χ.(6.1)

Since (γ⋅x)2=r2I(\gamma\cdot x)^2=r^2I(γ⋅x)2=r2I, its density is

ρ=ψ†ψ=A2(1+r2/a2)1−d.(6.2) \rho=\psi^\dagger\psi=A^2(1+r^2/a^2)^{1-d}. \tag{6.2} ρ=ψ†ψ=A2(1+r2/a2)1−d.(6.2)

Equation (6.2) is a density of squared field magnitude. It follows by multiplying the profile by its conjugate transpose; the terms linear in γ⋅x\gamma\cdot xγ⋅x cancel, and the Clifford square gives the remaining radial factor. The next equation asks a different question: which differential equation does this shape satisfy? Its right-hand coefficient depends on the field's own density, so the equation is nonlinear.

Direct differentiation gives

Dψ=da(1+r2/a2)−1ψ=gρ1/(d−1)ψ,gA2/(d−1)=d/a.(6.3) D\psi=\frac d a(1+r^2/a^2)^{-1}\psi =g\rho^{1/(d-1)}\psi,\qquad gA^{2/(d-1)}=d/a. \tag{6.3} Dψ=ad​(1+r2/a2)−1ψ=gρ1/(d−1)ψ,gA2/(d−1)=d/a.(6.3)

The word stationary here means that a spatial equation has been solved. No time dependence has yet been supplied that would identify the particle's temporal frequency. An action or variational functional assigns a number to a field configuration; requiring its first change to vanish under all allowed small field variations produces an Euler–Lagrange equation. The functional F\mathcal FF in (6.4) is a spatial example, distinct from a complete spacetime action. Its specially chosen nonlinear power is called critical in this bubble construction. That choice is part of the equation being tested, not a depth-independent master law already established for all particles.

For example, the derivative of the radial prefactor contributes −dxi/[a2(1+r2/a2)]-dx_i/[a^2(1+r^2/a^2)]−dxi​/[a2(1+r2/a2)] times that prefactor; using the Clifford square combines the scalar and vector terms into (6.3). This is a stationary critical nonlinear Dirac equation. It is the variation with respect to ψˉ\bar\psiψˉ​ of

F=∫Rd[Re⁡(ψ†Dψ)−g(d−1)dρd/(d−1)]ddx.(6.4) \mathcal F=\int_{\mathbb R^d} \left[\operatorname{Re}(\psi^\dagger D\psi) -\frac{g(d-1)}d\rho^{d/(d-1)}\right]d^dx. \tag{6.4} F=∫Rd​[Re(ψ†Dψ)−dg(d−1)​ρd/(d−1)]ddx.(6.4)

Critical Dirac bubbles are established mathematics; see Borrelli, Malchiodi and Wu, Ground State Dirac Bubbles and Killing Spinors. The equations above specify the flat spatial version used here. They do not import a probabilistic interpretation.

6.2 Why the Entire Pattern Has Half Spin

Rotating a spatial pattern has two parts: transform its component values and rotate the positions at which they are evaluated. In (6.5), R−1xR^{-1}xR−1x handles the coordinates and U(R)U(R)U(R) handles the spinor components. The equation says that both changes together are equivalent to rotating only the seed label of this particular profile. This is an intertwining relation: the explicit spatial construction preserves the seed's transformation law.

A rotation generator gives the infinitesimal change produced by a small rotation. The three JiJ_iJi​ below describe rotations about an observer's three chosen axes. Their squared sum is a Casimir operator, a combination unchanged by those rotations. For a spin-sss representation its value is s(s+1)s(s+1)s(s+1) in these dimensionless units, so 3/43/43/4 identifies s=1/2s=1/2s=1/2. The exponential tests the finite 2π2\pi2π rotation. This proves a transformation property, not an absolute integrated spin normalization or a spin-statistics law.

For a spatial rotation R and its spin lift U(R), Clifford covariance gives

U(R)ψχ(R−1x)=ψU(R)χ(x).(6.5) U(R)\psi_\chi(R^{-1}x)=\psi_{U(R)\chi}(x). \tag{6.5} U(R)ψχ​(R−1x)=ψU(R)χ​(x).(6.5)

Thus rotating both coordinates and components acts on the whole profile through the seed spinor. On an observer three-plane choose J1=−iγ2γ3/2J_1=-i\gamma_2\gamma_3/2J1​=−iγ2​γ3​/2, cyclically. These satisfy

The induced total rotation, including the derivative of spatial arguments, therefore has spin one-half. Ignoring that derivative would calculate only the component contribution and miss part of the pattern's angular momentum. The seed spinor premise already contains the half-angle law; the additional result is its realization in this full nonconstant spatial profile.

A profile is normalizable when its integrated squared magnitude is finite. This asks whether its long tail contributes a finite amount, not whether the field has a hard edge. In radial coordinates the volume element includes a factor rd−1r^{d-1}rd−1; decay of the density must be strong enough to overcome that growing volume. Neither a nor A is discretized by this calculation. Its nonlinearity changes with d. Consequently it does not yet derive all these profiles as branches of one common ten-space action or select their mass frequencies.

6.4 Integer-Spin Channels and Photon Polarization

A bilinear expression uses two field factors, for example ξξ†\xi\xi^\daggerξξ†. Its rotation law need not be the same as the law of either factor alone. The Pauli matrices σ1,σ2,σ3\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3σ1​,σ2​,σ3​ form a basis for traceless Hermitian two-by-two matrices. Together with the identity they split the bilinear into a scalar part sss, unchanged by rotations, and a vector part vvv, which rotates as an ordinary three-component vector. Their Casimir values distinguish spin zero and spin one.

Polarization concerns how field components oscillate in a physical plane. Complex coefficients conveniently encode their relative phases. Transverse means perpendicular to a specified spatial wave-direction vector KKK. Helicity is the rotation weight about that direction in the observer's three-dimensional description; it is not synonymous with the whole spin representation. The symbol E⊥E^\perpE⊥ denotes directions perpendicular to the plane EEE. These definitions make the photon comparison below precise without replacing the project's photon picture by an exchanged particle.

7. A Different Result: Which Minimal Spinors Admit a Clock?

The preceding theorem concerned rotation of a spatial shape. This chapter asks a different question: which minimal component systems permit a rotation-invariant time-evolution term with one time derivative? That kinetic requirement supplies a more selective depth test under its own premises.

7.1 The Invariant Alternating Form

This calculation asks which real component systems can carry a rotation-invariant first-order time term. A module is simply a component space together with the specified action of a group or algebra. “Irreducible” means it cannot be split into smaller nonzero invariant component spaces; “minimal” chooses the smallest spinor system of the stated type. The word fibre, used below, refers to components at a physical point. It is not a separate physical manifold.

The commutant is the set of all linear operations that commute with the prescribed rotations. Real Schur theory says that for this irreducible situation the commuting algebra is real, complex or quaternionic. Those names specify multiplication rules for real matrices: R\mathbb RR, C\mathbb CC and H\mathbb HH. Quaternions have three independent imaginary directions with square minus one. None of these algebras changes real physical spacetime.

A real matrix is skew when JT=−JJ^T=-JJT=−J. It defines an alternating pairing, for which qTJq=0q^TJq=0qTJq=0. Nondegenerate means that no nonzero component vector is paired to zero with everything else, equivalently that JJJ is invertible here. Such a JJJ can supply a first-order clock; a degenerate one leaves directions without that time term. The table counts which invariant choices exist under the minimal-module premise.

In even spatial dimension the spinor rotation representation can split into two chiral branches, distinguished by the sign of an oriented product of Clifford matrices. Choosing one chirality chooses one such branch. This algebraic chirality is defined relative to the stated spatial construction; it is not automatically the observed left- or right-handed interaction behavior of a particle.

Let V be one minimal irreducible real Spin(d) module. Seek a nondegenerate real skew matrix J commuting with every rotation of V. With the invariant positive inner product, real Schur theory gives the commuting division algebra R, C or H. Their skew subspaces have dimensions zero, one and three. In the latter two cases a normalized nonzero skew element squares to -I.

7.3 The Essential Carrier Qualification

A carrier is the complete set of field components on which the proposed equations act. Restricting which spatial rotations are considered does not automatically remove components from that carrier. This is why a theorem about one minimal spinor cannot be transferred unchanged to a larger field containing several copies. The distinction affects which clocks are allowed, not just how they are named.

A full ambient field restricted to a lower depth need not be minimal. The real 32-dimensional Spin(10) half-spin module restricts with repeated copies; its skew commutant dimensions at seven, eight and nine are 6, 2 and 1. Those copies restore clocks. An even number of real-type copies can pair into an invertible skew form. Second-order dynamics also evade the first-order criterion.

The later massive Clifford field has complex dimension 32, or real dimension 64. Calling that field and the minimal real module the same carrier would be incorrect. A common physical theory would need to isolate the minimal active pattern used in the selector while retaining the full kinetic structure needed by its spatial evolution. This isolation is open.

7.4 Independent Color Restricts the Clock without Removing It

Here color is introduced as a transformation rule for three component labels. The group U(3)U(3)U(3) consists of complex three-by-three matrices preserving the norm of a three-component vector. The subgroup SU(3)SU(3)SU(3) additionally has determinant one. A triplet is its basic three-component representation; a singlet is unchanged by every transformation. The number three counts representation components. The number eight counts the independent infinitesimal generators of SU(3)SU(3)SU(3). These are different counts.

A group describes allowed operations and how they compose. Topology describes global properties such as connectedness and holes of a space or pattern. Calling a transformation rule SU(3)SU(3)SU(3) does not assign an SU(3)SU(3)SU(3)-shaped topology to physical space or to a particle. Although a group itself can be studied geometrically in mathematics, this manuscript uses its matrix action on coefficients of the one spacetime field. It introduces no group manifold as a physical arena. Nor does a color label by itself derive a force or a gluon; IDWT's interactions must come from the same field.

A spin doublet has two complex component labels. Independent color means that the color transformation commutes with the chosen spin transformation. Their combined labels give C2⊗C3\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^3C2⊗C3, six complex entries or twelve real entries; those entries require a physical field realization and are not twelve spatial directions. The Hilbert–Schmidt matrix norm is the square root of the sum of squared absolute matrix entries. Equation (7.5) uses its square, with the indicated real normalization. This measures a commutator's failure to vanish and does not introduce a Hilbert-space ontology.

For a quark candidate with observer spin doublet and independent color triplet, use C2⊗C3\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^3C2⊗C3 as a real module. 8. Why the Complete Middle-Hodge Channel Has Three Components at Three/Four

8.1 The Rank Theorem

This chapter uses another way to describe oriented spatial data. A one-form is a linear rule that assigns a number to a tangent vector, such as extracting its component along an axis. A two-form assigns signed values to oriented area elements; higher forms extend this idea to higher-dimensional oriented elements. Their components are antisymmetric: exchanging two directions reverses the sign. The notation ΛmV\Lambda^m VΛmV denotes the degree-mmm exterior forms or equivalent exterior components, using the Euclidean metric to identify the relevant vector and covector descriptions.

The wedge product, ∧\wedge∧, combines such oriented elements antisymmetrically. Repeating a direction gives zero. A basis wedge of independent directions is called a blade. In 2m2m2m directions an mmm-form has middle degree: its complementary oriented element also has mmm directions.

The Hodge star uses the physical Euclidean metric and an orientation to send each oriented element to its perpendicular complement. In three dimensions it relates an oriented area to its normal direction; in four dimensions it sends two-forms to two-forms. Applying it twice gives the sign in (8.1). A Hodge eigenform is a component combination carried into a multiple of itself by that operation. The two eigenspaces are the chiral channels used here. When the eigenvalues are +i+i+i and −i-i−i, the complex notation encodes paired real components; it does not change physical space.

“Complete channel” means that every component in one such eigenspace is retained. “Shadow” means the specified relation between the odd-dimensional data and its containing even-dimensional spatial channel, not a second physical space. This relation is an additional premise. The normal covector n♭n^\flatn♭ in the next paragraph evaluates the component along a chosen unit normal. Its nnn is unrelated to the mass-level index nnn.

8.2 A Spatial Triple Is Not Yet Independent Color

Three components can carry different transformation laws. An ordinary real spatial vector has three entries, but its rotations are SO(3)SO(3)SO(3). A complex color triplet carries the SU(3)SU(3)SU(3) action defined in section 7.4, with eight independent generators. Matching the number three does not identify these groups or supply independent color transport.

Here normal means perpendicular to a selected spatial subspace. A four-base is a chosen four-dimensional subspace within physical ten-space, leaving six perpendicular directions. It is a reference split of the same space, not yet the bound/free split of an identified particle. Three pairs of those six directions can be encoded using C3\mathbb C^3C3. The exterior degrees zero through three have 1,3,3,11,3,3,11,3,3,1 component labels, totaling eight; this explains the factor eight in (8.4).

Parity of exterior degree means whether that degree is even or odd. A normal Clifford matrix changes that parity, which is why projecting to one fixed degree can erase required normal derivatives.

The infinitesimal generators of a continuous group form its Lie algebra, with commutators recording how small transformations combine. The lowercase notation su(3)\mathfrak{su}(3)su(3), or su(3) in prose, denotes the algebra of SU(3)SU(3)SU(3). Similarly SU(2)SU(2)SU(2) consists of determinant-one unitary two-by-two matrices and supplies the double-cover rotation law for a spin doublet. An algebra of three spatial rotation generators is not an algebra of eight independent color generators.

A real triple of middle-form components rotates as a spatial vector in the three-dimensional shadow. Its rotation algebra has three generators, not eight. If three equivalent complex modes possess independent norm-preserving and volume-preserving transport, their algebra is su(3). That equivalence and transport are physical premises to realize.

Independent slots cannot be introduced merely to avoid that zero without specifying their field origin.

9.2 What Can Select the Six Normal Directions?

The charge table used six normal directions as an input. This separate argument asks whether another geometric requirement singles out that number. 10.2 What the Repair Has and Has Not Solved

A free equation contains no additional interaction term. A conserved label of that equation must be retested after an interaction is added. It must also have the required behavior under translating a whole isolated pattern: ordinary electric charge should not change because the coordinate origin changes. The next two tests separate these requirements from the already proved free commutator.

This is an exact conserved free-field generator, with suitable decaying domains. It is angular about a selected origin. Higher base angular degree ell changes its spectrum by multiples of ell/3; spin one-half and radial density do not automatically select ell=0. Translations generally fail to commute with this origin-dependent Q. A local interaction also need not preserve it even if ordinary total angular momentum is conserved.

A reciprocal interaction evolves all participating field components through the same action; no profile is merely a fixed external receiver. A centroid is the spatial center defined by the chosen density. Ordinary torque measures the change of total spatial angular momentum. Because QangQ_{\rm ang}Qang​ contains a more particular spin-orbital combination, zero centroid displacement and zero ordinary torque need not make its derivative vanish.

There is a concrete reciprocal counterexample. For the same-field contact V=λρ2/2V=\lambda\rho^2/2V=λρ2/2, take three orthogonal positive-beta Gaussian components of width L centered in a base plane at (b,0),(0,b),(−b,−b)(b,0),(0,b),(-b,-b)(b,0),(0,b),(−b,−b), with the reviewed polarization signs (1,-1,1). Recentring the origin on the centroid cannot cure this example. It is a failure of that particular interaction to conserve the proposed charge, not a theorem against every possible reciprocal same-field interaction.

Another possible repair is to start with a constant component label in a basis where free positive- and negative-energy branches are separated, then transform it back to the original field variables. The Foldy–Wouthuysen map W(p)W(p)W(p) performs that free change of component basis at each momentum ppp. Conjugating an operator means Q0↦WQ0W†Q_0\mapsto WQ_0W^\daggerQ0​↦WQ0​W†. The physical electric source remains open: a generator, its continuity current, a source law for Psi, reciprocal conservation and a common classical normalization must be demonstrated together. Multiplying a free component weight by an arbitrary field norm does not derive the observed equal charge of the electron, muon and tau.

12. Localization, Same-Field Tails and Complete Inertia

The algebraic properties do not remove the need for a sustained physical object. Recent work supplies a separate positive-action localization candidate. It is included because it tests that requirement constructively, not because its action has already been joined to the first-order spinor.

12.1 A Fully Specified Comparison Action

A numerical solution has two separate tests: whether its discretized equations are solved accurately, and whether those discrete solutions approximate the continuum problem. A residual is the value left when a proposed solution is substituted into the equation; a small residual concerns that equation and its chosen normalization. A grid weights errors differently near an axis, which is why a small weighted residual can conceal a larger pointwise error.

The Hessian is the second variation of the constrained energy. Positive values on a specified set of perturbations mean that energy increases to quadratic order in those directions. Testing only real amplitudes does not test every complex component, shape, singlet or dynamical perturbation. Likewise, being below a dispersal threshold means that spreading into the stated comparison configuration costs more energy; it is not a proof against every decay channel. These distinctions govern the results after the table.

The dispersal threshold is 3. Two finest extrapolations suggest 2.43910. Real-amplitude Hessians were positive on the tested 32,64,96 grids; pure spatial phase changes have exact nonnegative gradient cost. These are restricted tests, not full stability. A weighted optimizer residual hid axis errors; sparse Newton correction on 96/192 grids reduced pointwise discrete residuals below 1e-12 with energy changes below 3.4e-11 per P. Those are discrete equations and convergence estimates, not continuum existence certificates.

The component frequencies are approximately 0.718715 and 0.780906. This is a two-phase relative equilibrium: its shape is stationary while the two component phases advance at their separate rates. It is not yet a particle made of C copies of one fundamental. P is continuous and not selected. No measured mass, physical depth or quantized charge follows from these numerical profiles.

Localization also requires the directional forces within a pattern to balance. A norm-preserving dilation stretches the profile while reducing its amplitude enough to keep its integrated norm fixed. 13. Do the Shared Assumptions Fit Together?

13.1 A Dependency Map

The preceding chapters do not all start from the same action or component carrier. A compatibility witness is an explicit construction in which selected assumptions and results coexist. It is stronger than noticing similar numbers, but weaker than showing that one physical solution realizes every property. The table distinguishes those levels by listing each result's additional inputs beside its output.

The common depth assignments are a meeting point, not the only premise. The following table makes the extra dependencies explicit.

13.2 Explicitly Compatible Choices

The useful question is what happens when the ingredients are actually combined. Does a shared choice preserve both properties, introduce a new constraint, or destroy one of them? The examples below show combinations that have been checked. Their conclusions stay at the algebraic or source-action level where the checks were performed.

First, simplex count and color/spin multiplicity need not compete. On a chosen polynomial band the model spectral label can be μdS(n,d)Ispin⊗Icolor\mu_dS(n,d)I_{\rm spin}\otimes I_{\rm color}μd​S(n,d)Ispin​⊗Icolor​. It is invariant under both actions; a color triplet does not multiply the frequency by three. This is a mathematical compatibility witness, not a derived physical mass operator. If a proposed feedback instead traces over every component, its normalization has to explain why that extra factor is absent.

Second, an independent color triplet and spin doublet coexist while restricting the clock to an ordinary complex direction, as (7.5) proves. The combined assumptions produce a further constraint rather than a contradiction. This is stronger than listing separately compatible ranks.

Third, retaining the full kinetic field and projecting only the bilinear source permits spatial chirality, independent color and a positive three/four contact to coexist in (8.7)–(8.11). The construction gives a single explicit source rule across all assigned depths, with its shadow premise stated. It demonstrates more than coincident terminology.

Fourth, the determinant branch changes normal U(1) charge but leaves SU(3) representation type unchanged. It accounts simultaneously for a charged singlet, a neutral singlet and two equally colored triplets. That is a shared algebraic choice producing several outputs without four independent charge assignments.

Fifth, the actual angular repair combines total spatial spin, both base branches and normal charge on one full kinetic field. The spin and charge operators are not just unrelated matrices attached afterward. Its known interaction defect, however, prevents calling this a finished physical charge theory.

13.3 Bridges That Remain Necessary

A bridge is a derived relation between two candidate descriptions: for example, a reduction showing that the components and conserved quantities of one action obey the equations used in another. Reusing the same letter, charge table or spatial dimension is not such a relation. The outstanding bridges below identify precisely what must connect the useful constructions.

The minimal real clock fibre and the full massive complex Clifford field are different hypotheses. Minimal active-fibre isolation might reconcile them, but it has not been derived. One cannot apply the selector to the large field while silently discarding its clock-restoring multiplicities.

The normal six-plane in the charge construction and the electron's bound six-plane are different subspaces. They coexist geometrically, but identifying them would change the construction. Likewise the pure pencil does not generate all intermediate bound directions, and preserving a fixed nested flag reduces literal normal rotation symmetry.

Spatial Hodge indices and independent color indices are different. Their joint current is explicit, but matching the integer three never suffices to identify their transformations. The fixed zero-order normal color commutant test also differs from total angular color that rotates coordinates; its depth restrictions cannot be transferred to the latter without checking.

The positive second-order localization action supplies different equations and canonical charges from the first-order Clifford construction. Its numerical profile has two phase velocities. No common reduction currently lets it inherit the first-order half-spin/charge proofs or the one-fundamental portion law. The problem is a missing bridge, not that the useful individual results are false.

Classical norms remain continuous. Relative charge weights, half-angle transformation and a mass-frequency label do not separately fix their absolute integrated source strengths. A common physical normalization is needed wherever spin, charge and inertia are compared quantitatively.

13.4 The Joint Evidential Claim

Several consequences of one premise can be explanatory without being statistically independent. If the same geometric choice produces both a clock restriction and a charge structure, that is a reason to test the common choice more deeply. It is not permission to multiply arbitrary success probabilities. The joint claim is therefore about explicit mathematical constraints and demonstrated compatibility, not numerical odds for the theory.

The shared assumptions are compatible at several demonstrated algebraic and source-action levels. There is no established single action realizing every row of the table at once. That is the present answer to the compatibility question; assuming complete compatibility would overstate it, while treating each successful calculation as isolated would understate it.

The interest is the concentration of constraints. The count ladder, finite spinor profile, clock criterion, complete Hodge rank, independent normal color and determinant charge rule repeatedly intersect the same proposed depth organization. They make a structured programme with explicit tests. Some results share hypotheses and are correlated. Their number cannot be converted into numerical odds by multiplying arbitrary success probabilities. Section 5.3 separately quantifies the joint numerical mass-and-ratio event under an explicit reference distribution and the fixed prescription. Its conditional coverage is not a numerical probability for the combined physical theory, and the correlated geometric results are not multiplied into it.

14. What the Programme Has Established and What Would Complete It

The exact mathematics includes the simplex identities, the conditional assignment certificates, full-profile spin covariance and norm integrals, minimal-module clock classification, complete middle-Hodge rank theorem, color contractions, exterior charge weights, free differential charge conservation, conjugate map and the stated stress/response identities. Each has its hypotheses above. Numerical localization is supporting calculation under a declared action, with restricted stability and discretization limits, rather than an existence proof.

The suspected physical picture is a common field sustaining finite patterns of different spatial involvement, with a kind-specific fundamental and count-proportional registered frequency. The same geometry may control which patterns support half-spin, independent color and the relative charge blocks. Deterministic trajectories describe particle centres; internal oscillations and detector averages remain separate. Same-field response produces interactions without exchanged particles.

The compact-profile results in sections 12.6–12.8 add exact support, a finite restricted energy basin and a mechanical clock construction under explicit premises. They do not replace the geometric property proofs or establish that one field solution realizes all of them.

The central unfinished derivation is a common spatial dynamics that selects the occupied n, sustains C common-frequency portions, preserves the physical charge/color source under encounters, and matches the sector-scale prescription with consistent normalization. Required tests include the actual bound/free support, full 10+1 response, the neutral five-depth branch, equal charged-lepton electric response, finite-lived versus persistent branches, and full reciprocal energy/momentum balance. Resolving bottom, neutrino absolute scale and physical antipattern identification remains part of the programme. No completed mass operator or experimental confirmation is claimed.

The case for further investigation does not require pretending these tasks are finished. It rests on reproducible relations, reusable geometric choices, and explicit constructions that can be extended or falsified. The next decisive advance would be a tested common action closing several of those bridges without independently adjusting each particle.

Appendix B. Explicit Matrix and Operator Recipes

B.1 Clifford Matrices and the Charge/Spin Calculation

This recipe turns the abstract Clifford relations into explicit small matrices. A tensor power means repeated tensor products; an exponent zero means that factor is absent. Each Pauli matrix has two rows and columns, so five factors give 25=322^5=3225=32 rows and columns. This is a component-matrix size, not a spatial dimension. The “occupation” numbers in this recipe label exterior degree algebraically, not counted physical particles.

Let X,Y,Z be the ordinary Pauli matrices and I the two-by-two identity. For q=0,...,4, construct

γ2q+1=Z⊗q⊗X⊗I⊗(4−q),γ2q+2=Z⊗q⊗Y⊗I⊗(4−q).(B.1) \gamma_{2q+1}=Z^{\otimes q}\otimes X\otimes I^{\otimes(4-q)},\quad \gamma_{2q+2}=Z^{\otimes q}\otimes Y\otimes I^{\otimes(4-q)}. \tag{B.1} γ2q+1​=Z⊗q⊗X⊗I⊗(4−q),γ2q+2​=Z⊗q⊗Y⊗I⊗(4−q).(B.1)

They are 32-by-32 Hermitian matrices. A normalized product proportional to all ten provides beta. For each normal pair define occupation na=(I−iγ2a+3γ2a+4)/2n_a=(I-i\gamma_{2a+3}\gamma_{2a+4})/2na​=(I−iγ2a+3​γ2a+4​)/2, a=1,2,3; thus the normal spin sum is ∑ana−3/2\sum_an_a-3/2∑a​na​−3/2. Project onto even total normal occupation j=0 or 2, form Gamma4 as in (10.2), and diagonalize (3Γ4/2+∑ana−3/2)/3(3\Gamma_4/2+\sum_an_a-3/2)/3(3Γ4​/2+∑a​na​−3/2)/3. The multiplicities must be 2 at -1, 6 at -1/3, 2 at 0 and 6 at 2/3. The matrices −iγ2γ3/2-i\gamma_2\gamma_3/2−iγ2​γ3​/2 and cyclic permutations have squared sum 3I/4 and commute with this restricted Q. These operations reproduce the lowest-angular charge/spin table without referring to a named particle.

To reproduce the differential identity rather than just its lowest matrix, apply D4X4+X4D4=2E4+4D_4X_4+X_4D_4=2E_4+4D4​X4​+X4​D4​=2E4​+4 to a smooth test spinor and use [E4,D4]=−D4[E_4,D_4]=-D_4[E4​,D4​]=−D4​. Substituting B4 from (10.2) gives B4D4+D4B4=0B_4D_4+D_4B_4=0B4​D4​+D4​B4​=0. Multiplication by the anticommuting Gamma4 then gives [K4,D4]=0[K_4,D_4]=0[K4​,D4​]=0. Normal gammas commute with Gamma4 and B4, while total normal rotations commute with the normal Dirac contraction. This proves the full free commutator, including every spatial derivative. Boundary conditions must still make integrated generators well-defined.

B.2 A Small Exact Way to Reproduce the Real Clock Table

The entries in the following words label real two-by-two matrix factors. Counting commutation signs lets the clock commutant be found without solving a large approximate linear system. “Bitwise XOR” is a discrete operation on the labels that records matrix multiplication up to a sign; the explicit skew and commutation rules retain the signs relevant to the test.

Real matrix words avoid a large symbolic nullspace. Use the real basis I,X,Z,AI,X,Z,AI,X,Z,A, with A=(0−110)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(01​−10​), labeled 0,1,2,3. Distinct nonidentity letters anticommute. Tensor words commute when the number of positions containing distinct nonidentity letters is even; they are skew exactly when they contain an odd number of A letters. Product labels are bitwise XOR, up to an irrelevant sign.

For the quaternionic four-real-component module use generator words (3,0), (2,3), (1,3). Seven mutually anticommuting real eight-by-eight negative-square generators are

(3,0,0), (2,3,0), (2,2,3), (2,1,3),
(1,0,3), (1,3,1), (1,3,2).

Spin(5), Spin(6) and Spin(7) use pair products from their first five, six and seven generators. A chiral Spin(8) uses all seven and their pair products. For Spin(9), prepend A to each of the seven and append X tensor I8 and Z tensor I8, obtaining nine positive-square generators on R16; their pair products generate rotations. For Spin(10), prepend Z to those nine and append X tensor I16, then take pair products on R32. Enumerating all words commuting with these rotations and counting the skew ones gives the table in section 7. Spin(2) uses A, and Spin(1) is scalar. This is an exact finite computation of the minimal-module commutants. It does not justify minimality as a physical premise.

B.3 Hodge, Color and the Joint Clock Check

An increasing index subset chooses an oriented basis blade. The complementary subset supplies the Hodge partner, and the permutation sign records their orientation. In the color recipe, EijE_{ij}Eij​ is the matrix with one in row iii, column jjj, and zeros elsewhere. A Gram matrix collects inner products between the commutator matrices; its diagonal form records the squared failure of each clock direction to commute with color, including the zero mixed terms.

Enumerate increasing m-index subsets I of {1,...,2m}. The star matrix maps each basis blade to its complementary blade with the sign of the permutation (I,I-complement). Squaring it gives (-1) to the m times I; its transpose has the same parity sign. Half its dimension is the rank in (8.3). The construction uses physical Euclidean spatial forms only.

For an explicit normalized color basis take, for each i<j, (Eij+Eji)/2(E_{ij}+E_{ji})/2(Eij​+Eji​)/2 and (−iEij+iEji)/2(-iE_{ij}+iE_{ji})/2(−iEij​+iEji​)/2, and the two diagonals diag(1,-1,0)/2 and diag(1,1,-2)/(2 sqrt(3)). These eight Hermitian matrices reproduce (8.5) entry by entry. Tensoring them with the identity on the spin doublet and converting a complex matrix M into (Re⁡M−Im⁡MIm⁡MRe⁡M)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\operatorname{Re}M&-\operatorname{Im}M\\ \operatorname{Im}M&\operatorname{Re}M\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ReMImM​−ImMReM​) gives the real twelve-by-twelve color action. Complex conjugation is diag(I6,-I6). Construct J0,J1,J2 as in section 7 and sum their commutator Gram matrix. It is diag(0,10/3,10/3), proving (7.5), including the absence of mixed terms.

B.4 Running and Retrieving the Evidence

Download the finite-calculation program and save it as particle-geometry-checks.py. Python with NumPy and SymPy is sufficient. Running

python particle-geometry-checks.py

writes particle-geometry-checks.json beside the program and prints its pass status and executed source hash. The public program preserves the exact reviewed calculation bytes; the repository's resource allocator is only an operational execution aid, not a dependency of these finite formulas. The joint mass-and-ratio appendix separately provides its complete input data and two programs. The clock-connectivity proposal has its own checker and explicitly different review status.

Primary source hashes below identify the historical geometric baseline, not the revised November text. The displayed equations and recipes are sufficient to reproduce the finite comparisons without access to the private research catalog. The large localization solve is specified by its action, measure, boundary prescription and convergence tests; the small checker does not rerun it.

The scalar, clock, Hodge and color tests in this program are finite identities. Numerical matrix comparisons check the finite instances to the stated tolerance, with the general proofs given in the text. They are not tests of actual particle trajectories, a physical field amplitude, full nonlinear stability or agreement with every experimental observable.

Appendix C. Combined Glossary and Index

This appendix defines terms and symbols and points to their first substantial explanation or calculation. The section links are the locators; no page numbers are assumed. A symbol can have several meanings in different candidate constructions. Those meanings are listed explicitly rather than being silently identified. All component and representation language describes the one field on ordinary physical 10+1 spacetime.

C.1 Concepts and mathematical tools

Term Meaning in this account Where to read
Conditional joint coverage Fraction of a stated comparison distribution satisfying all absolute-mass and ratio bounds together, with observed thresholds and fixed model choices. 5.3
Importance sampling Sampling acceptance regions directly and correcting their known sampling density to measure a rare union. 5.3
Joint precision event One mass list satisfying every individual and within-family ratio requirement under a single admissible assignment. 5.3
Overlap multiplicity Number of admissible assignment/rung regions containing the same mass list; inverse weighting avoids counting it several times. 5.3
Sampling confidence and arithmetic guard Finite-sample uncertainty and a separate numerical-error qualification; neither is uncertainty in the physical theory. 5.3
Action; Lagrangian A functional whose stationary variation gives field equations. A spacetime action integrates a Lagrangian density; a spatial functional alone does not establish time evolution. Spatial example, 6.1; component action, 12.1
Adjoint representation; octet The transformation rule for a group's own generators. SU(3)'s adjoint has eight components. This count is distinct from a triplet's three. 8.2
Alternating form A bilinear pairing that changes sign when its inputs are exchanged; on equal inputs it vanishes. The real clock uses an invertible skew matrix representing such a pairing. 7.1; normal bilinear, 9.2
